question: A 32-year-old man comes to the Veterans Affairs hospital because of difficulty sleeping for the past 9 weeks. He is a soldier who returned from a deployment in Afghanistan 12 weeks ago. Fifteen weeks ago, his unit was ambushed in a deserted street, and a fellow soldier was killed. He wakes up frequently during the night from vivid dreams of this incident. He blames himself for being unable to save his friend. He also has trouble falling asleep and gets up earlier than desired. During this period, he has started to avoid walking in deserted streets. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. He refuses cognitive behavioral therapy and is started on sertraline. Five weeks later, he returns to the physician and complains about persistent nightmares and difficulty sleeping. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms persisting despite sertraline therapy" -> "Persistent nightmares and difficulty sleeping" -> "Consider adjunctive therapy targeting nightmares and sleep disturbances" -> 80% CHAIN: "Persistent nightmares and difficulty sleeping despite sertraline therapy" -> "Symptoms suggestive of PTSD-related sleep disturbances" -> "Consider pharmacological intervention targeting PTSD-related sleep disturbances" -> 75% CHAIN: "Persistent nightmares and difficulty sleeping despite sertraline therapy" -> "Symptoms suggestive of PTSD-related sleep disturbances" -> "Initiate prazosin therapy as an adjunct for PTSD-related nightmares and sleep disturbances" -> 80%
analysis: The patient is presenting with symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) following a traumatic event during his deployment. Sertraline, an SSRI, is a first-line treatment for PTSD. However, since the patient is still experiencing persistent nightmares and difficulty sleeping despite being on sertraline, the most appropriate next step in management would be to add prazosin therapy. Prazosin is an alpha-1 adrenergic antagonist that has shown efficacy in reducing nightmares and improving sleep in patients with PTSD.
